notes.meaning: Moses tells Israel not to be terrified when they face an enemy with more soldiers, horses, and chariots. God's people were mostly foot soldiers, while their enemies had powerful war chariots. They could still be bold because the Lord who brought them out of Egypt was with them.

Before battle begins, a priest steps up to encourage the troops. He tells the men not to faint, tremble, or panic before their enemies. True victory does not come from human strength, because the Lord Himself marches with His people to fight for them.

Officers dismiss any man who built a new house but has not yet dedicated it with a family blessing or feast. God shows kindness to people's ordinary lives, letting a man enjoy what he worked for before facing danger. A soldier with an unsettled home might also be distracted in the fight.

A man who planted a vineyard was excused from battle if he had not yet tasted its fruit. Under God's law, a farmer waited until the fifth year to freely use the fruit of a new vineyard. God cared about His people's labor and did not want them to miss the joy of their harvest.

A man engaged to be married was released from military duty so he could return home to his bride. An engagement was a binding covenant, and it would be a deep sorrow to die in war before starting life together. God wanted His soldiers to serve willingly rather than with divided hearts.

The officers also excused anyone who was terrified or fainthearted. Fear spreads quickly in an army and can make other soldiers lose their courage. By sending frightened men home, the army was kept strong in faith and united in purpose.

Once the excused men had left the camp, the officers appointed captains to lead the remaining troops into battle. Good order and bold leaders were needed so the soldiers could fight effectively. Trusting God for the outcome does not replace having wise human leadership in place.

When Israel marched against an enemy city outside Canaan, they were required to offer terms of peace first. If the city opened its gates and surrendered peacefully, the people were spared and put to work paying tribute. God taught His people to seek peace and avoid needless bloodshed whenever possible.

If a distant city refused peace and chose to fight, the Israelites surrounded it and laid siege. Once the Lord gave them victory, they were commanded to put every fighting-age man to the sword. This severe measure punished the city for choosing war and prevented future rebellions against Israel.

differ.view: Reformed teaching often sees the command to kill all the men as a temporary concession to human hardness of heart, falling short of God's perfect law of love while still restraining greater cruelty.

notes.meaning: The women, children, farm animals, and goods of the captured city were not destroyed, but kept as plunder. God allowed the soldiers to use these goods to supply their needs and support their families. This rule showed a measure of mercy by sparing the lives of non-combatants.

God makes it clear that these rules of offering peace and sparing non-combatants applied only to distant cities. They did not apply to the nations living inside the Promised Land itself. Different rules were needed for the land Israel was inheriting to protect them from dangerous idolatry.

In the cities of the Canaanite nations, Israel was commanded to leave alive nothing that breathed. God ordered this total destruction because these nations practiced terrible sins, like child sacrifice and idolatry. Removing them completely was God's severe judgment, and it protected Israel from adopting their corrupt practices.

During a long siege, Israel was strictly forbidden to chop down fruit trees to build war equipment. Trees take years to grow and provide vital food for everyone, both during and after the conflict. A fruit tree is not an enemy soldier fighting back, so soldiers had no right to ruin it.

The soldiers were allowed to cut down only wild trees that did not produce food. They used this timber to build siege works, such as ramps and battering rams, until the hostile city fell. Even in the heat of war, God required His people to show restraint and preserve the land's resources.
